paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: the fear you rehearse is not always the welcome you get. Jacob lined up his family, sent gifts ahead and bowed seven times, because he had spent years bracing for the worst (Genesis 33:1-3). Then Esau ran to him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him, and they both wept (Genesis 33:4). I have rehearsed a whole speech in my head before a hard conversation, and the other person just said, "Come in, sit down."

Notice what Jacob says when it's over. He tells Esau, "I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably" (Genesis 33:10). He also says, "God has been gracious to me and I have all I need" (Genesis 33:11). I think Jacob knows he didn't earn this welcome, and he gives God the credit for the kindness. When someone shows you grace, friend, say thank you, and let it point you to the God who is gracious first.

Then look at how Jacob finishes. He doesn't rush to follow Esau. He goes on at a pace his children and livestock can handle (Genesis 33:13-14), and then he arrives safely at Shechem and sets up an altar (Genesis 33:18-20). A hard thing got settled, and the very next thing Jacob does is worship. So when God brings you through something you dreaded, baker, go slow, take care of the little ones in your life, and build your own altar, even if it's just a quiet minute of thanks.
